passage: John laughs at me, of course, but one expects that in marriage
text:
The narrator says her husband John mocks her beliefs about the house, and she treats this as a normal part of being married to someone who doubts her.

She notes that John laughs at her suspicions that the house is strange, and she accepts this as the ordinary way a husband treats his wife's fancies. The tone is wry and resigned, not angry.

The line matters because it establishes the power imbalance at the heart of the story. John is a physician who dismisses her feelings as nervous weakness, and her acceptance of his mockery shows how much she has absorbed his authority. Her later doubts about his judgment grow out of this early dismissal.

passage: I am sitting by the window now, up in this atrocious nursery
text:
The narrator is sitting by a window in the upstairs nursery, which she calls atrocious, and she is writing there. This is on page 3.

She is alone at the window and free to write because her husband John is away at work all day. She is in the room they have rented for the summer, which was once a children's nursery and playroom, and she dislikes it. The word "atrocious" signals her strong disgust with the room, and the bars on the windows and the marks left by children hint at its history.

The sentence also reveals her situation: she writes in secret, against her husband's orders to rest and avoid work, so the room becomes both her confinement and her only space to think.

passage: It is the same woman, I know, for she is always creeping
text:
The narrator is sure the figure she keeps seeing outside is the same woman she has seen behind the wallpaper, because the figure is always creeping, and most women do not creep in daylight. The sentence sets up her reasoning for linking the woman outdoors to the woman in the pattern p. 10.

What it says: she has seen a creeping figure in the lane, the arbors, and the road, and she concludes it is one and the same woman, identified by her habit of creeping rather than by any face or detail.

What it means here: the narrator's certainty comes from a pattern in her own perception, not from evidence. Her earlier fears about John, Jennie, and the paper suggest her judgments are shaped by her confined and unstable state, so the reader should treat her conviction as a sign of her distorted mind rather than as a reliable observation p. 10.

passage: I think that woman gets out in the daytime
text:
The narrator believes the woman she sees behind the wallpaper escapes the room during daylight hours.

The sentence is the narrator's conclusion from her nightly watching. She has noticed that the woman creeps behind the pattern and shakes it, and that she is trying to climb through. Her next lines report that she has seen the woman outside, creeping along the lane, through the garden arbors, and along the road, so the claim rests on what she thinks she has observed.

Within the story this belief marks a turn toward fixation and unreliable perception. The narrator's husband, John, has told her the fancies are false, yet she treats the figure as real and as escaping. Her confidence here signals how far the wallpaper has taken hold of her mind.

passage: Personally, I disagree with their ideas
text:
The narrator's disagreement with her physicians could be read as mere self-assessment, yet the text gives her grounds to be doubted as a judge of her own condition.

The objection is that her claim to know better is undercut by her own description of her state. She writes that she "cry[s] at nothing, and cr[ies] most of the time" p. 5, and that she is "getting dreadfully fretful and querulous" p. 5. A critic would argue that the narrator's self-report is unreliable because her distress is the very thing under question, so her disagreement with the physicians counts as a symptom rather than an independent medical opinion. The document also records her confession that "I did write for a while in spite of them" p. 1, showing that her preference for work is tied to the secrecy and conflict she describes. Her authority is further weakened by her admission that "I am getting a little afraid of John" p. 8, which suggests her perceptions of the people around her are themselves strained.

The author's best reply, drawn from the text, is that the narrator presents her disagreement as sincere and explains why she is silenced: the men "say the same thing" and dismiss her, so her protest is the only voice available to her p. 1.

passage: John laughs at me, of course, but one expects that in marriage
text:
The strongest objection is that the narrator's dismissal of John as a mere skeptic ignores that his scepticism is a reasonable response to her own unreliable self-report.

John laughs at the narrator's suspicion of the house, and she writes that "one expects that in marriage" p. 1, presenting his mockery as ordinary marital teasing. A careful critic would object that this framing lets her treat his disbelief as personal temperament rather than evidence. Her own account describes her as "sly," crying "at nothing," and sleeping little while hiding wakefulness p. 8, so her claims about the room are the very thing John has grounds to doubt. The objection is that the passage casts a reasonable physician's skepticism as mere laughter.

The author's best reply is that the passage is a first-person record in which the narrator's perception is meant to be taken seriously, so John's laughter is shown only as one character's view, not the text's verdict.

passage: I have locked the door and thrown the key down into the front path
question: Why does she throw the key away?
text:
The narrator gives her reasons right after the line: "I don't want to go out, and I don't want to have anybody come in, till John comes. I want to astonish him." p. 12 So the immediate purpose is privacy. She wants to finish stripping the paper and free the woman behind it without Jennie or anyone else interrupting, and she wants John to see the result himself.

Throwing the key away goes further than locking the door. It makes the lock impossible to undo from inside, so she cannot be talked or coaxed out, and no one can enter without breaking the door down or finding the key.

It also matters later. When John pounds and calls for an axe, she tells him the key is "down by the front steps, under a plantain leaf," and repeats it until he goes to fetch it p. 12. That keeps him out long enough for her to be found in her new state, and it lets her feel she controls the encounter for once.

The document doesn't say whether she planned this as a trap for John. That reading is an inference from what she does.

passage: He says that with my imaginative power and habit of story-making
question: Is John right about her imagination?
text:
The document gives good reason to doubt him, though it doesn't settle the matter outright. John's claim is that her "imaginative power and habit of story-making" will turn a nervous weakness into "excited fancies" p. 3. He treats imagination as the cause of her illness and prescribes suppressing it, which is why he forbids writing, visitors, and even thinking about her condition.

The narrative shows the opposite effect. She says writing would "relieve the press of ideas and rest me" p. 4, and that having to hide it exhausts her. Isolation, enforced rest, and a barred nursery seem to feed her fixation on the wallpaper rather than cure it. Her fancies grow from the pattern's "dim shapes" into a creeping woman p. 7, and by the end she creeps around the room herself p. 13.

Still, she does see things that aren't there, including women creeping outside p. 10, so his worry about delusion isn't baseless. The document doesn't say what her condition actually is. The diagnosis of "nervous depression" is only John's and her brother's claim p. 1. Whether her imagination caused the decline or his treatment did is left for the reader to judge, though the text leans toward the latter. That reading of Gilman's intent comes from general knowledge of the story's critique of the rest cure, not from the text itself.

passage: It is the same woman, I know, for she is always creeping
question: Who is the woman in the wallpaper?
text:
The document never says outright who she is, so what follows is interpretation built from the text.

Within the story, the narrator first sees her as a dim shape behind the front pattern, "like a woman stooping down and creeping about behind that pattern" p. 7. By the passage you've selected she believes the woman gets out in daylight, and she sees her creeping along the lane, the arbors, and the road p. 10. Sometimes she thinks there are many women behind the paper, sometimes only one p. 10.

The most common reading is that the woman is the narrator's own projection. The pattern's bars echo her confinement: the barred windows, the schedule, the forbidden writing, John's control. She creeps because she is hidden and ashamed of being seen, just as the narrator hides her writing and locks the door when she creeps by daylight p. 10. The ending supports this, since the narrator says "I've got out at last" and has taken the woman's place p. 13. The story also hints that the woman stands for women generally, given the "great many women" and the creeping figures outside p. 12. Those readings come from critical interpretation, not from anything the narrator states.

question: Who is Jennie and how does she treat the narrator?
text:
The document never says outright who Jennie is. She is a member of the household who manages things for the narrator: "Jennie sees to everything now" p. 5, and she is the one getting the house ready for their return p. 7. The narrator also mentions John's sister, "a perfect, and enthusiastic housekeeper" p. 4, so Jennie may be the same person, but that is an inference. The last page has the narrator say "in spite of you and Jane" p. 13, and the document doesn't explain that name.

Jennie is kind and unobtrusive in the narrator's own account. She "is good and lets me alone when I want her to" p. 5. When the narrator catches her with a hand on the wallpaper, she says it stains clothes and asks them to be more careful p. 9. She tells John the narrator sleeps a lot by day p. 11, offers to sleep in the room with her, and says she wouldn't mind pulling the paper down herself, though the narrator mustn't get tired p. 11.

The narrator reads all this as scheming, and she calls Jennie "sly." Nothing Jennie does in the text, though, goes beyond ordinary care and concern.

question: How does the narrator's view of the wallpaper change over the story?
text:
Her view moves from disgust, to fascination, to a secret she guards, to identification with what she sees in it.

At first she finds it simply hideous. She calls it "one of those sprawling flamboyant patterns committing every artistic sin" and its color "repellant, almost revolting" p. 2. John refuses to repaper the room p. 3, and she says she would hate it herself if she lived there long p. 2.

Then it begins to hold her. She is "getting really fond of the room in spite of the wallpaper. Perhaps because of the wallpaper," and she follows the pattern for hours p. 5. She notices a sub-pattern behind the front design p. 5, which she decides is "like a woman stooping down and creeping about behind that pattern" p. 7. By night the outer pattern becomes bars p. 8.

Next it becomes hers alone. She suspects John and Jennie of studying it, is determined that "nobody shall find it out but myself," and refuses to leave until she has solved it p. 9. She also credits it with making her feel better p. 9.

Finally she merges with it. She believes the woman shakes the pattern and tries to climb through p. 10, helps her peel it off p. 11, and sees herself creeping in the long smooch along the wall p. 12. Her last claim is "I've got out at last" p. 13.

question: Why does John faint at the end, and what does the narrator's last line suggest?
text:
The document never gives a reason. The narrator herself asks, "Now why should that man have fainted?" p. 13. So any explanation is interpretation, though the text supports a few.

The plainest reading is shock. He has told friends there is "nothing the matter" but "temporary nervous depression" p. 1, and has insisted she is "better, dear, whether you can see it or not" p. 7. He then breaks in and finds her creeping along the wall, the paper stripped, and she tells him "I've got out at last" p. 13. His cry, "For God's sake, what are you doing!", shows his horror p. 13. His confidence as a physician collapses in front of him.

Her last line, that she "had to creep over him every time," suggests a reversal of power p. 13. John has governed her schedule, her room, her writing and her visitors. Now he lies in her path and she passes over him without concern. That can be read as triumphant liberation or as complete breakdown, and the story leaves both open. Her freedom is also confined to the room, where she follows the smooch on the wall p. 12.

Before you start
×

A woman, confined by her physician husband to a rented summer mansion for a supposed nervous condition, keeps a secret journal. Her fixation on the yellow wallpaper of her nursery room grows as the story moves through the summer.

Where we are

A couple rent a secluded colonial mansion for the summer; the narrator is forbidden to work and told to rest because of her "nervous depression." p. 1
They live in a former nursery at the top of the house, with barred windows, a bed fixed in place and peeling, repellent yellow wallpaper. p. 2
The narrator writes in secret, since her husband and his sister disapprove. The rental runs three months, so time is limited. p. 7

People

The narrator — Unnamed writer of the journal, a wife and new mother, treated as an invalid and cut off from work and company.
John — Her husband, a practical physician who dismisses her fears and directs her every hour.
Jennie — John's sister, a devoted housekeeper who looks after the household and the narrator.
Mary — The nurse who cares for the narrator's baby.
